transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-08-21
Start time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Laura Chen (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Samir Desai (Redwood Runtime Eng); Priya Nair (BlueCap ML Lead), Jonah Green (BlueCap Infra), Sofia Vega (BlueCap Product), Alex Kim (BlueCap Security)
Recording note: automated transcription, some mis-attributions, occasional garble.

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be imperfect):
- Deep dive on overhead introduced by constrained decoding / JSON-mode and function/tool calling for structured outputs; impact of KV cache hits, batching, and quantization on end-to-end tail latency and throughput.
- Agreed to run customer-specific benchmarks in an ephemeral VPC and an on-prem staging node.
- Next steps: SE to run benchmarks, customer to share prompts and VPC access notes; Redwood will provide cost delta and SOC2 docs.

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Laura Chen: All right thanks everyone for joining, um we'll just get started. I'm Laura from Redwood, i'm the AE on this account. Marco and Samir are with me. Priya and team, thanks for taking the time.
[00:00:22] Priya Nair: Yeah hi thanks. We want to focus this session on the runtime impact of strict decoding constraints — json-only mode plus function calls — and how that mixes with batching and quantization. Latency is critical for our realtime routes.
[00:00:35] Marco Ruiz: Great, that's exactly what we planned to cover. Quick agenda: 1) measured overhead of constrained decoding and structured-output enforcement; 2) KV cache behavior and prefix reuse; 3) batching tradeoffs for p99 vs throughput; 4) quantization interactions; 5) infra/vpc/on-prem constraints.
[00:00:50] Jonah Green: Quick note: our infra is hybrid, majority in our VPC on AWS but we need an on-prem node for sensitive customers. We'll need to know if Redwood's runtime can run 1) in our VPC with KMS support, and 2) as an on-prem runtime with similar perf profile.
[00:01:10] Samir Desai: Yep, we've got a private deployment pathway. The runtime binary supports KMS integrations for envelope keys and HSM workflows; we can also provide an on-prem appliance image. Performance parity depends on the host GPU and network between control plane and inference nodes.
[00:01:28] Sofia Vega: From product side — key success is matching our 200ms p95 for the 4k prompts. If json-mode pushes us to 300-400ms that's a problem. Also accuracy regressions matter: constrained decode mustn't break structured fields.
[00:01:45] Marco Ruiz: Understood. I'll start with the constrained decoding overhead numbers we collected in our lab. Caveat: these are model and hw dependent.
[00:01:57] Marco Ruiz: Example: Llama-3-8k baseline unrestricted decode on A100-80GB, 1 request, no batching: mean per-token latency X. When we enable strict-json enforcement (forced token set + constrained beam rules) we observed a 12-18% token-time increase, and end-to-end latency grew about 10-25% depending on sequence length due to additional token-filtering and checks in the decode loop.
[00:02:25] Priya Nair: 12-18% token increase — is that mostly CPU overhead for the constraint logic or does it change GPU kernels?
[00:02:34] Samir Desai: Mostly CPU + decode loop overhead. We do a token mask / allowed-list calculation and that hits the host, but we also reduce speculative execution so fewer wasted tokens. On small batch sizes the CPU portion becomes visible — that's why we prefer colocated SE threads or optimized C paths in the runtime.
[00:02:53] Jonah Green: So if we push more batching, does that amortize the CPU cost?
[00:03:02] Marco Ruiz: To an extent yes. Batching increases GPU utilization so the relative CPU overhead drops. But for strict p95 requirements we can't batch too long. Our tests show sweet spot: batch sizes 4-8 for 4k sequences on Ampere hardware — p95 improved vs batch=1 and throughput scaled up. But p99 tail can worsen if you wait for batch fill time.
[00:03:23] Priya Nair: Did you test prefix KV cache with structured output — like repeated few-shot prefix? We rely heavily on cache since many of our prompts share the same prompt-engineering header.
[00:03:36] Marco Ruiz: Yes. KV cache hits reduce compute heavy sections and token generation time by up to 30% when prefix length is long. Caveat: when you use constrained decoding with dynamic allowed token sets per step, the cache still helps for the model's attention ops, but the per-step CPU token filter still runs. So net benefit remains, but slightly attenuated.
[00:03:54] Alex Kim: Any impact on cache encryption or KMS calls? We need to ensure KV cache in ephemeral on-prem nodes doesn't leak keys.
[00:04:02] Samir Desai: KV cache is ephemeral in-memory. If you use KMS for model weights or checkpoint decryption, that's separate. Our recommended pattern is to use local envelope keys for runtime and integrate with your KMS for key unwrap. We don't make frequent KMS calls during inference.
[00:04:20] Marco Ruiz: Another dimension: quantization. We ran experiments with 8-bit, 4-bit quant profiles. 8-bit gives minimal accuracy delta and 20-35% lower token cost. 4-bit (sym & GPTQ-style) offers larger cost savings but sometimes increases latency slightly due to suboptimal kernel pathways and additional dequant steps, especially for attention softmax where precision matters.
[00:04:41] Priya Nair: So 4-bit might reduce cost but could increase p95? That's counterintuitive for us — we assumed quant always helps latency.
[00:04:50] Samir Desai: Right — depending on the kernel implementation on the hardware, 4-bit may force slower emulation or bit-unpacking steps. On some stack/compiler combos we see a 5-10% p95 increase but substantial throughput gains for batched workloads. On newer tensorcore kernels it's often a win, but we need to bench on your exact GPU.
[00:05:10] Sofia Vega: How about tool/function calling overhead — when we call an external tool mid-generation or use function schema enforcement, what's the round-trip model? We do a lot of synchronous tool calls that must return quickly.
[00:05:23] Marco Ruiz: Good question. Redwood supports function-call integration where the model emits a structured function call token stream. The runtime can optionally short-circuit output and return the structured payload without continuing generation. The overhead depends if you do a blocking external call: if tool call is external HTTP it adds network latency. If it's internal (local microservice) it's less. Also we can use partial decode to stop the generation once the function call is detected which saves tokens.
[00:05:46] Priya Nair: For us, function-call outputs are often validated against a JSON schema. Does the decoder do schema validation inline?
[00:05:55] Marco Ruiz: We do optional inline validation for common constraints; heavy validation is recommended off-model. Inline schema checks are light-weight (field existence, token set constraints) and add marginal CPU time. They help catch structural errors early.
[00:06:09] Jonah Green: Can you quantify the end-to-end overhead of function calls vs plain text?
[00:06:15] Marco Ruiz: Roughly: pure text path baseline p95 = 180ms (4k context, batch=1 on A100). JSON-mode w/ inline validation and forced token sets = +20-30% => ~220-240ms. If you add synchronous external tool call (100ms avg network + processing) you hit ~320-350ms. But we support asynchronous tool invocation patterns and prefetching to hide latency.
[00:06:43] Priya Nair: Those numbers are helpful. The 100ms external is an example — our internal tools are <50ms usually.
[00:06:50] Marco Ruiz: Then your end-to-end should fit your 200ms p95 if you use short tools plus caching.
[00:06:56] Samir Desai: Another optimization: partial prefix caching of the function-call detection head. If many prompts invoke the same function signature, the runtime can cache the early logits progression; that reduces the detection latency.
[00:07:12] Sofia Vega: About quant + KV cache interaction — does quantized KV cache degrade results?
[00:07:18] Samir Desai: We keep KV cache in the format that's optimal for the runtime. For 4-bit we often store dequantized floats for the cache to avoid repeated dequant ops, or we use a compressed-float format with fast kernels. That said, memory footprint changes. We have toggles depending on your memory/latency tradeoffs.
[00:07:35] Priya Nair: On the VPC/on-prem deployment side: will the observed lab numbers translate to our on-prem GPU (NVIDIA H100 80GB)?
[00:07:45] Marco Ruiz: H100 usually outperforms A100 for mixed precision and quantized paths, so it's likely you'll see better or comparable throughput and latency. We'll run the benchmark on your H100 if you grant access. We need to test both 8-bit and 4-bit kernels and ensure the compiler stack (CUDA + cuBLAS/cuTENSOR versions) matches.
[00:08:01] Jonah Green: Security question: can the on-prem runtime operate disconnected from Redwood control plane?
[00:08:07] Samir Desai: Yes, air-gapped option exists. We ship a private control plane that runs in your network with limited callbacks. For telemetry we can buffer and forward via secure channels. RBAC and audit logs are retained locally if required.
[00:08:21] Alex Kim: Good. Also need to see KMS integration details — we can't allow keys to leave VPC.
[00:08:26] Laura Chen: We'll include our KMS integration doc in the package. Marco will also annotate recommended IAM roles for the ephemeral benchmark nodes.
[00:08:34] Marco Ruiz: Quick note on batching strategy: we recommend hybrid dynamic batching with latency-aware thresholds — e.g., flush if waiting >35ms or batch size reaches 6. That keeps p95 low while recovering throughput in bursts. For strict p99 you might prefer fixed small batches and more capacity.
[00:08:52] Priya Nair: Do you have a tool to simulate our traffic shape? We have a tail-heavy pattern with bursty interactive users.
[00:08:59] Marco Ruiz: Yes we can run a traffic replay harness against your sample traces and simulate latency SLOs and autoscaling triggers. We'll need a few days to configure it for your routes.
[00:09:08] Sofia Vega: On accuracy/regression monitoring — if we quantize aggressively, will Redwood detect and alert on semantic/regression changes?
[00:09:16] Samir Desai: Redwood Optimize ties quality metrics to prompt sets and evals. We run A/B tests, compare embeddings and n-gram/semantic similarity, and surface potential regressions. We'll set up an eval suite for your canonical prompts.
[00:09:30] Priya Nair: Good — that's key for our product sign-off.
[00:09:35] Marco Ruiz: Ok, wrapping to next steps: we'll run the constrained-decode + quant + batching bench on your H100 and in a VPC staging. We'll attach raw logs and a tipping-point analysis (when quant helps vs hurts).
[00:09:49] Jonah Green: Timeline?
[00:09:52] Marco Ruiz: We can start once Priya shares sample prompts and Jonah grants ephemeral VPC credentials — aiming for raw results by 2025-08-28.
[00:09:59] Laura Chen: I'll send the runbook and SOC2 bundle after this call.
[00:10:04] Priya Nair: Great, thanks. Any other open questions?
[00:10:09] Alex Kim: One more: pricing implications — can you give a rough per-inference delta for 8-bit vs 4-bit with batching?
[00:10:17] Marco Ruiz: We'll produce a model: per-token compute cost drops ~25-45% with 4-bit depending on kernel; per-request cost depends on tokens generated and effective batch size. We'll include a worked example for your average prompt.
[00:10:30] Sofia Vega: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[00:10:33] Laura Chen: Okay we'll follow up with artifacts. End call.

(Transcription continues with some verbatim Q&A clipped, and technical notes appended)

Appendix (notes, rough numbers):
- Baseline single-request p95 (A100): ~180-220ms for 4k average prompt, batch=1.
- JSON-mode (forced token set + inline validation): +10-30% end-to-end latency.
- KV cache hit: up to ~25-35% savings on token generation when prefix is long.
- Batching: batch sizes 4-8 often best for throughput vs p95 on Ampere; hybrid dynamic batching recommended.
- 8-bit quant: 20-35% cost savings, latency neutral or slightly better.
- 4-bit quant: up to 50% cost savings in some workloads, may add 5-10% p95 on some stacks; wins on newer tensor cores.
- Function call path: stops generation early when function detected; external tool latency dominates if sync calls used.
